item.title: ChatGPT Pro’s biggest perk just got cut in half. Meet the new AI subscription math
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 1.14
OpenAI unveiled several flashy new features during its annual developer’s conference Tuesday, from the always-on “Dot” work agent to a new, cloud-based security system that keeps constant watch for cyber threats. But one of the biggest — and to many ChatGPT users, the most infuriating — headlines from DevDay wasn’t announced on stage. The news centered around the $200-a-month ChatGPT Pro 200 plan, which the company had paused for new signups earlier this month due to demand for GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s most powerful and token-hungry model. First, the good news: OpenAI said it was taking new signups for the Pro 200 plan again. The not-so-great news? The plan’s relative usage limits compared to the $20-a-month ChatGPT Plus plan were being greatly reduced. Welcome to another edition of Prompt Mode, your weekly AI newsletter. I’m your host, Ben Patterson. Each week on Prompt Mode , I’ll be serving up analysis of the AI trends that matter to everyday users like you and me. Stay tuned for practical AI tips, hands-on experiences with the latest AI tools, and–you guessed it–prompts to help you get the most out of your AI assistants. Thanks for reading, and if you like what you see, just sign up right here . Previously, the Pro 200 plan got you 20 times more usage than Plus plan, but according to a rough chart shared by OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux on X , the $200-a-month Pro plan will now only offer 10 times the usage limits of Plus, a 50-percent reduction. (Existing Pro subscribers are getting a brief grace period along with usage credits to smooth things over.) Naturally, those explanations aren’t going over too well in the ChatGPT community , with some users cancelling their subscriptions in protest. OK, so why is this happening? Sottauix, the Head of Core Products at OpenAI, served up a few different explanations, including the debut of new DevDay functionality that demand “a lot of compute,” while noting that OpenAI passed on the chance to “compromise in other ways,” including the reintroduction of a rolling five-hour usage limit. More importantly, Sottauix pointed out the recent 50-percent API rate cut for two of its newer and more efficient models, GPT-6 Sol (which already has a successor in GPT-6.1 Sol) and GPT-6 Luna. (API rates are essentially pay-as-you-go, versus opting for a flat subscription rate.) “We don’t want to put an incentive on ourselves to artificially inflate the API list prices to make it look like [subscribers] are getting a lot (and workaround it through discounts, etc),” Sottauix wrote. “Instead we want to continue to both rapidly reduce prices and increase capabilities of models on the API.” The result for Pro 200 subscribers getting their usage limits chopped in half is essentially a wash, although as Sottauix promises, “we guarantee that over time you always get more work done and with an increasing level of quality … as a result of models getting more efficient.” Sottauix also hinted at the addition of “more things to the subscription that won’t draw on the usage,” which turned out to include chats with OpenAI’s new Dot assistants. Still, the changes to OpenAI’s Pro 200 plan point to a trend we’ve been tracking for months : namely, the big AI providers endlessly tinkering with their flat-rate subscription plans to keep pace with ever-changing and increasingly powerful AI features, particularly the token-heavy agentic ones. Expect more of the same in the weeks and months to come. More in AI this week Here’s more about ChatGPT’s Dots, which are geared less toward home use and shopping and more toward collaborating at the office . [PCWorld] Google finally took the wraps on its revamped frontier Gemini model , Gemini 4 Aragon. Google-provided benchmarks look impressive, but the new model is being limited to “trusted testers” before rolling out to the general public. [Google] Gemini Gems are going away, but Gemini skills — which were formerly reserved for paying Gemini Spark users — are replacing them, and they’ll now work for free users . [PCWorld] President Trump has announced a “morally binding” accord with AI leaders over safety , while announcing that artificial intelligence should henceforth be called “super intelligence.” I’ll just leave it at that. [Reuters] Bill Gates sat down for Ezra Klein’s podcast to expand on his AI worries. If you’re looking for reassurance about AI apocalypse fears, you won’t find much here . [New York Times] Meta’s Muse AI agent has run headlong into various privacy snafus, including one in which it sent the home address of a user (who had asked Muse to take charge of his Facebook Marketplace account) to a complete stranger. [The Verge] Prompt of the week: The “don’t build until I say” prompt Claude Sonnet 5.5 has arrived, and with it comes a prompt that could help keep any AI agent from leaping into action before making a plan first. The prompt, which comes directly from Claude maker Anthropic , concerns “open-ended” requests, including those that don’t strictly define boundaries for what the AI should and shouldn’t do. Specifically, the prompt can help keep Sonnet and other AI models from spinning up charts, videos, and other “artifacts” when all you really wanted was just a plan. That’s all for now! Thanks for reading the latest issue of Prompt Mode. Want more next week? Don’t forget to sign up to start receiving this newsletter in your inbox.

item.title: Best PDF editors: Premium, budget, and free options
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
PDF files are a necessary component of our multi-platform world. With this convenient file format, users are able to view and share documents across various devices, using various operating systems and software programs. While tasks such as simple viewing and/or commenting on a PDF can be accomplished with free software, there are times when you need a broader range of tools for working with a PDF document. He’s a veteran tech journalist who has been reviewing and writing about hardware, software, and services for a variety of publications including TechHive, Wired, Macworld, Mac|Life, Mobile Magazine, Enterprise.Nxt, Executive Travel, and others. He was formerly PCWorld’s Small Business Editor. A word about online PDF editors Why spend a chunk of change on a desktop editor when free online PDF editors abound? The simple answer is because you get what you pay for. Generally, free online editors will let you add text and comments, merge and split documents, and convert files to and from PDF. With rare exception, however, they won’t let you edit existing text and many have file-size and page-volume restrictions. And a lot of them will watermark your edited document. For these reasons, web PDF editors are best reserved for simple, fast editing jobs. Call in these big dogs for anything more demanding. How to choose the best PDF editor PDF editors come in a variety of flavors, offering varying feature sets—from basic functionality to power-user tools. It’s important to know what features best match your workflow before you commit to a PDF editor. Create, convert, and export PDFs The most fundamental function of a PDF editor is to make PDFs, either from scratch, scanned hard copies, or by converting digital documents. A good PDF editor should be able to transform a variety of file types—from Microsoft Office formats to images to HTML—and do so seamlessly, preserving the original formatting. It should also include OCR technology to make the PDF text searchable and editable. Likewise, a good PDF editor must be able to export PDFs into other editable formats such as Microsoft Word and PowerPoint, HTML, or plain text, maintaining the original files hyperlinks, images, and other elements. Content editing Another bit of magic that PDF editors unlock is the ability to modify text; insert, resize, and move images; and reorganize pages in the PDF. A good one will perform these tasks as easily as in a text document or slide deck, allowing in-line editing, dragging-and dropping graphics, and adding or removing hyperlinks. Review and annotate A good PDF editor should also let you or anyone else using it add comments and other annotations to PDF files during review. It should have tools to mark up both text documents and graphic-heavy files like webpages. Common options include sticky notes, callout boxes, highlighting, freehand drawing tools, and stamps with messages like “approved,” “revised,” and “confidential.” Security All businesses deal with documents containing sensitive data. Look for a PDF editor that includes security features that allow access for authorized eyes only. Good options will usually offer several levels of security, including password protection, permissions setting, and content redaction, which “blacks out” selected text and images. Most PDF editors will also offer one or more ways to electronically sign documents. Mobile support While deep PDF editing is best done on a desktop, it’s nice to be able to review and annotate files when you’re out and about. While PDFs can typically be reviewed in any PDF reader or editor, regardless of which one they were created in, consider looking for an editor that has a dedicated mobile app, is optimized for mobile devices, or allows cloud access to features through a mobile browser. One of the great things about a PDF is that it can be read and edited in any PDF program regardless of which one it was created in. So beyond the features outlined here, let your personal preferences guide you in making your decision. FAQ 1. What is the best PDF editor? If you want a PDF editor that truly does it all, PCWorld’s pick is Adobe Acrobat Pro . It’s the industry standard for a reason. As a subscription-based product, you can count on it to always be up to date, in terms of patches and feature enhancements. That also grants you access to a mobile version that’s both robust and user friendly. 2. What is the difference between a PDF document and a PDF form? While there are a number of different types of PDF file formats, they all fall under the umbrella term of PDF documents. A PDF form is a type of PDF document that has editable form fields a user can fill out. Typically, parts of the document are static and can’t be changed in a PDF form, such as questions in a survey or instructions about filling out the form. In a PDF form, the content fields a user fills out are open to editing and can offer a list of possible answer options or can be written in freely. 3. Are PDF documents and Word files different? Yes. They are two entirely different document formats. While you can export from one file format to another, they are not the same. Word file formats are usually used for word processing, editing, and making changes to text. PDF documents on the other hand, are most often utilized for viewing, sharing, and printing. Additionally, Word files are read and write and contain some version of the “.doc” file format. Whereas PDF files are typically read-only and contain the “.pdf” file format. 4. Can you protect PDF documents from being edited by other people? Yes. If you have a PDF document that you don’t want anyone else to edit, you can protect the file. You can do this by opening the file in Acrobat, for instance, and clicking Tools > Protect . Then you have a few options as to whether you want to simply restrict editing with a password, or if you want to encrypt the file for further safety. Once you choose how you want to protect the PDF document, you can set a password and save. 5. Can you merge PDFs with a free PDF editor? As a matter of fact, many free PDF editors allow you to merge two or more PDFs into one document. Such is the case with our top free pick PDF Candy. Open up the PDF editor application or website in your browser and search for the Merge option. It will then ask you to add the files of all PDFs you wish to merge. Once the files have been added, arrange the page order and alignment before proceeding with the merge. Afterwards, all of your previously PDF files will be merged into one new PDF document. 6. Does Google have a free PDF editor? Yes and no. Google doesn’t provide a designated free PDF editor itself, but there are third-party Chrome extensions that you can use to help get the job done. Alternatively, you can make use of Google Drive to edit a PDF document. Simply upload the document onto your Google Drive and then select the file and right-click and select Open with > Google Docs . The file will be opened as an editable Google Docs text document. Then just make your edits and when you’re finished click File > Download >PDF Document to revert it back to a PDF file. This method is a quick and easy way to edit a simple PDF document, but be careful as Google Docs can run into formatting issues if your original document has complex visual formatting such as tables and graphs. In this case, it is best to use a designated free or premium PDF editor. Related content Adobe Acrobat Standard vs. Acrobat Pro: When does spending more make sense? Log your Days. Log your life. AI Voice Recorder with a Personal Context System Soulog Sense There’s a particular kind of frustration that anyone juggling meetings, classes, or creative projects knows well: the good idea that slipped away because you were too busy talking to write it down, the client detail buried somewhere in a call, the lecture point you meant to revisit but never found again. Live Rewind cannot retrieve audio from before the feature was enabled. As with any recording feature, users should make participants aware and comply with applicable recording and consent laws. Soulog From Recording to Understanding What sets Soulog Sense apart isn’t just what it captures, but what happens afterward. Powered by Soulog APP, from Capture → Structure → Understand → Connect → Create → Publish , the system doesn’t just transcribe—it works to understand meaning, connect related context across sessions, and generate structured outputs like summaries, key points, action items, owners, and open questions. Instead of searching through hours of audio for one useful moment, users can ask questions across that accumulated material and trace the response back to its source. For the professional moving between calls, the parent trying to hold onto small family moments, the student trying to truly listen instead of transcribe, or the creative chasing an idea before it disappears, that connection is the point. Capture what matters. Let Soulog keep it together. Turn it into something you can use. Online backup is your protection against any harm that might come to your computer or local storage devices. Mechanical failure, acts of malice, or natural disasters are serious threats to all of the data you have stored on your PC. While I always recommend keeping a local backup for quick restores (see our roundup of the best Windows backup software for desktop solutions), uploading your data to a cloud backup service is a good way to cover your bases. There’s a valid reason for the “ backup rule of three ,” which includes an offsite copy. Fortunately for consumers, there are myriad affordable and convenient online backup options, many with unique selling points. While my primary focus in this article is backup, I also discuss other roles that a cloud service can fulfill, such as document viewing and editing, file sharing, multiple-device support, and emergency-restore options. Note: You won’t see familiar names like Google Drive, OneDrive, or Dropbox on this list. Those are more accurately defined as synced cloud storage . Besides typically lacking a desktop client, and offering limited, if any, automatic backup functionality, online storage syncing involves mirroring — where any deletions or changes are reflected on the other end. Online backup uses versioning, so older data is retained — an important failsafe feature. Why you should trust PCWorld for online backup reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name, PCWorld. Our reviewers have been testing PC hardware, software, and services for decades. Said client software offers the same sync functions for free accounts as it does for paid tiers, which gives it a leg up over the free tiers of many other services. There’s also a local virtual drive à la Dropbox, Google Drive, and others. Icedrive: Further considerations While 10GB of storage isn’t enough for power users or businesses, if you’re simply looking to keep documents online with the ability to sync them across multiple devices for free, Icedrive is a reliable service with an excellent client. Plus, you can always upgrade to a paid tier for more storage as needed. That might not be as pricey as you’d think, though the discounted prices on the site are for the first year only. Annually, Icedrive is $29 for 2TB (discounted from $99), $49 for 4TB (discounted from $159), and $99 for 6TB (marked down from $269). Most users will be best off with the 2TB plan which is quite competitive. Note that those discounted prices are for the first year only, reverting to full boat after that. Read our full Icedrive online storage review Backup software with cloud backup/storage support Typically, we separate our reviews of cloud backup services from local backup software (as seen in our best Windows backup software roundup.) But those lines have been blurred with backup software that includes support for cloud backup and storage. The following are reviews of such hybrid offerings: Dropbox Backup : Dropbox Backup is a nice solution for one-person account users, despite surcharges for long-term version retention. MSP360 Managed Backup : Backup for multiple computers at a decently low fee. Local and online, file-based and imaging, along with disaster recovery are all provided via manageable local clients. R-Drive Image 7.3 : This backup program has expanded support for cloud storage services — including the Amazon S3 and S3-compatible repositories Iperius Backup Basic : This backup program offers power aplenty, but the learning curve and interface might occasionally flummox less-experienced users. EaseUS ToDo Backup 2025 : A full-featured program that ranks among the top; its free version is particular robust. Handy Backup 8.5 Professional : Top-notch features might’ve garnered an Editors’ Choice award had it been entirely glitch-free and a bit easier to learn. Ashampoo Backup Pro 26 : Overarching support for myriad backup chores with easy-to-understand wizards. Zinstall FullBack : Unique among backup programs, it offers full migration of backed up data and apps to a new OS installation — for a relatively steep price. Aomei Backupper Pro : A complete backup solution capable of preserving your important data both locally and remotely. Aomei Backupper Standard : A respectable free backup program, if you can tolerate the occasional ad. It’s cloud storage is affordable but can only be used for backups, no other data. Acronis True Image : Besides being feature-packed, including support for cloud backup storage, Acronis throws in protection against viruses and malware. Retrospect 19 Solo : We like that this backup program includes support for both proprietary and third-party cloud storage, but not its lack of disaster recovery. Retrospect 19 Desktop : The pro version to Solo’s consumer version, Retrospect Desktop covers all the bases, but has a steep learning curve and high price. Even local backup software that doesn’t offer a formal cloud component can be made to incorporate the most popular online storage services, using a cloud storage manager . The good news is that you have lots of options for putting together a comprehensive backup strategy including local and remote copies of all your data! How PCWorld tests and evaluates online backup services As noted above, the performance of online backup services will vary wildly according to their location and the network equipment between you and the data depository. We installed the software and backed up the same 2GB data set to check for any major issues or glitches in the client software. These are noted in the reviews. See our article on how PCWorld tests cloud backup services for all the details. Who curated this article Jon Jacobi has been dabbling in the computing arts since the days when that required flipping switches. He has witnessed data storage morph from punch cards and tape to solid state drives. He’s been using and testing HDDs, SATA SSDs, and NVMe SSDs for PCWorld for well over two decades. That necessarily includes the software and services that support data storage. To paraphrase a well-known commercial, you might say he’s seen a thing or two. How to pick an online storage and backup service Cloud backup has unique considerations. Familiarizing yourself with the following key areas can help you find the cloud backup service that best meets your needs. Capacity Obviously, you’ll need as much storage as you have data, plus a little, or possibly a lot, more if you want to track changes and save previous versions of files — if that’s supported. Some services keep multiple versions of files, some don’t. In many cases there’s a time limit. Price Nearly all online services charge differently depending on amount of storage involved. Uploads are free, but downloads may be limited. In some cases, there are upload and download charges. Read the fine print. Aside from the free tiers available from a service like Dropbox, pricing is fairly consistent across services, though you definitely get more capacity for your money from some vendors. Features As we mentioned previously, in addition to backup, you may want to share your files with others, work with them from mobile devices, or even edit them with office applications such as those available with Dropbox, Google, and OneDrive. If you do intend to work online, we recommend that you maintain a local copy as far-more-quickly-restored backup, as well as a hedge against Internet downtime. OS and device support Most services provide client backup software for the major operating systems (Linux, OS X, and Windows) and both Android and iOS. Make sure the service you sign up for supports your entire panoply of computers and devices. Privacy If you’re concerned about the privacy of your data, make sure you use a service that allows the use of a personal encryption key that you define. Do NOT lose it, as it is absolutely required to restore your data. Sadly, using your own key often limits the types of services (e.g., no mobile backup) available. If private encryption keys aren’t available, read the privacy policy, especially with the free services—there are significant differences. FAQ 1. What’s the best online backup? When it comes to the sheer volume of features, iDrive is the pick of the online backup litter. With honorable mentions to Livedrive for unlimited storage, and Sync.com for free storage with real backup features. 2. What’s the best cheap online backup? Much of the “cheap” equation depends on how much storage you need. Icedrive in its 10GB free incarnation is PCWorld’s top pick for small amounts of data, with 5GB Sync.com next in freebie line. If you’re wondering why no OneDrive, Google Drive, etc. it’s because they don’t offer backup functions. Dropbox now offers a backup function (beta), so that’s another runner-up. Just avoid the Teams version of Dropbox Backup, which moves data before actually backing it up. For up to 1TB of storage, the lifetime deal of $199 from pCloud is hard to beat. 3. How reliable is cloud backup? Generally speaking, data centers are backed up to the hilt, and some of the larger ones even back up to different geographical locations. Availability (hopefully 24/7) can also be important. Check for news of outages and the vendor’s own service blogs. All the services we’re aware of have been near-100 percent reliable. 4. What speed and data transfer rates should I look for? Speed in most cases these days is far more dependent upon the speed of your broadband connection than that of the online service, though the geographical location of the storage and the equipment in between can make a significant difference. Check the location of the service’s data servers if speed is important to you. Or, just give the trial a whirl and see if you can live with it. 5. How often should you schedule backups? Ideally, you should back up your data as often as possible. This is especially true if you are working on an important project or have data that you absolutely cannot afford to lose. It’s a good idea to automate the backup process and have the cloud service back up your data every hour or so. You might also consider real time (as files are changed), or continuous (more granular scheduling such as every 5 minutes.) 6. What’s the difference between cloud backup services and services like Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive? Services such as Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive are considered cloud storage services because they don’t offer local backup clients, but sync via a local virtual drive or web interface. A user must place their files onto the service’s cloud manually. A cloud backup service provides a desktop client with either versioning or retention of all the files you’ve backed up. Cloud backup service providers may also offer additional data security measures such as end-to-end encryption. 7. Is it safe to store my data online? Yes! All cloud backup services offer encryption of your data both during the transfer to and from your computer as well as while your data is stored on the provider’s servers. While this encryption stops others from being able to view your data, it doesn’t necessarily stop them from stealing it. Generally speaking, while not infallible, cloud backup services are one of the most secure options for storing your data. 8. Do you need to back up everything on your computer? You should at least back up all data that you can’t stand to lose. All devices will likely experience technical issues over time and oftentimes this leads to your data being lost from that device. So you should do regular backups of everything that is important to you. However, backup services typically offer more storage than most people can use, so it’s never a bad idea to safely store all of your data in case of emergency. 9. What’s the difference between sync and backup? Though there can be variations such as one-way and mirroring, sync is generally thought of as any change (deletions included) to a data set reflected on all the data repositories involved in the sync. The change can be made in any repository and will propagate to the others. That includes the source, the online storage, and any devices linked to the account. Backup, on the other hand, should be an immutable copy of your source data from a point of time. In practice, however, vendors may use what’s known as versioning, i.e. retaining older copies of files while using the most recent version as the file shown in the backup. The effect is largely the same as incremental backup and requires a lot less time and space. Alas, when versioning or even plain backup are involved, there may be limits on how long older versions and deleted files are retained. This isn’t true backup, but simply a safer version of sync that allows vendors to reclaim space after a period of time. The good news? Most users won’t really need those older files. For those that do, be careful which service you choose.

item.title: Anthbot N8 review: Leaf cleanup is where this mower stands out
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros Collects grass and leaves Automatic emptying is reliable Stable navigation via RTK and dual camera App comes with zones, profiles, and schedules Cons Noisy at 68 decibels Needs space to turn round Takes breaks to recharge Rainwater collects in the basket Our Verdict We tested the Anthbot N8, a robotic mower that collects grass clippings and clears leaves. It’s slower and louder than typical models, but its cleanup performance is hard to beat. Price at time of review This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Price Today Price When Reviewed $1,699 Best Prices Today: Anthbot N8 Retailer Price Anthbot $1699 View Deal $1699 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Robotic mowers almost always leave the clippings on the lawn, but the Anthbot N8 does it differently. It collects grass and leaves and deposits both at a location of its choosing. This means it’s not just another variant of a mulching mower, but a machine for yard owners who prefer a tidy lawn. Anthbot N8: Design and build quality Anyone seeing the N8 on the lawn for the first time might easily underestimate it. At 24 inches long, the body itself is still manageable. With the grass catcher attached, the robot measures just under 3.3 feet. The manufacturer states a net weight of 38.7 pounds, while the shipping box says it weighs over 33 pounds. Michael Rupp The build quality is impressive. The top of the body is light in color, while the bumpers and underbody are anthracite. A purple ring on the wheels adds a splash of color. The drive wheels, with their deep tread, grip well even on damp grass. On the top is a control panel with a red stop button, three membrane keys, a battery indicator, and four status LEDs for 4G, Wi-Fi, GPS, and warnings. There is no display. All settings are managed via the app. Michael Rupp At the front, there are two camera openings behind the bumper, with an LED headlight between them. The robot is IPX6-rated for protection against water jets and can be hosed down with a garden hose. The charging station is IPX5-rated, and the adapter delivers 42 volts at 168 watts. Michael Rupp Anthbot N8: Two mowing systems The N8 has two operating modes. These are not controlled by a switch in the app, but by the blade disc. The Cyclone system collects clippings. The flat disc is fitted with three blades, which are bolted to the edge and bent upwards at the ends, similar to the high-lift blades on a gas mower. As the blades rotate, the wings on them generate an airflow. The mower deck above them tapers in a spiral pattern and opens into a discharge chute at the rear. The disc acts like a blower. It lifts the blades of grass, cuts them, and carries the clippings and leaves into the grass catcher via airflow. Anthbot quotes a collection rate of up to 99 percent and 4,000 revolutions per minute. Michael Rupp The Particle system mulches. This cutting disc is fitted with six blades: three straight blades and three spoon-shaped ones. The spoon-shaped ones keep the clippings in motion, while the blades break them down so they’re blown backwards and fall between the blades. Michael Rupp The two rear attachments differ mainly at the bottom. The 6.1-gallon grass catcher is enclosed and collects the clippings, while the discharge deflector is open at the bottom, directing the clippings straight onto the lawn. Both attach behind a hinged rear panel, which can be opened with a single movement. The N8 recognizes automatically which attachment is fitted to the mower. In the app’s main menu, Mulching is greyed out as long as the grass catcher is fitted. Michael Rupp To change the disc, screws on the underside need to be loosened first. This is a bit fiddly, but it’s meant to ensure safety. You only need to change the disc once or twice a season. The collection disc comes fitted as standard. If you want to mulch, you’ll need to swap the blade. When buying replacements, keep in mind that the N8 uses two different blade types: curved ones for the collection disc and straight ones for the mulching system. Anthbot N8: Setup There are more individual parts in the box than with many robotic mowers. As a result, assembly takes a little longer, but is straightforward. Clipping the two rear attachments (collection basket and discharge deflector) into place is a bit fiddly, as they need to be clipped into the correct position on the wire frames. No screws are required. Michael Rupp The charging station’s cables run through plastic screw connectors and are color-coded: purple for power and green for RTK. When connecting them, make sure to tighten them gently. The charging pad should be placed near the lawn, plugged into a socket. The app requires about 6.5 feet of clear space all around it as well as a Wi-Fi connection. At the top end of the station, the contact unit protrudes from the housing with two round contacts; above this is a black-and-white marking consisting of a cross and arrows, which the robot mower’s camera uses for orientation when docking. Michael Rupp The RTK antenna is mounted on a pole with a three-pronged ground spike and requires a clear view of the sky. If you skip this step, the N8 will use NetRTK via mobile networks and obtain its correction data from the internet. The 4G service is free for one year. After that, it costs $35.99 for one year, $75.99 for two years, and $107.99 for three years. Setup is done via the app. You pair the robot via Bluetooth, enter the Wi-Fi details, check the firmware, and then create the map. Automatic mapping (in the ACC app) isn’t something you can do while lounging in a deckchair. Michael Rupp The app requires clearly defined lawn edges and for you to follow the robot. Alternatively, you can map manually and guide the robot along the lawn edges using two joysticks. Michael Rupp Before the first mowing session, the grass should be shorter than 3 inches. The app recommends working your way down in stages from 3 to 2, and then to 1 inch. In our case, it took three or four passes before we were satisfied with the result. Anthbot N8: Features and app The app is clearly laid out and offers plenty of features. You can set up to 30 zones, each with its own name, and adjust the cutting height, mowing direction, and camera detection sensitivity separately for each one. The cutting height ranges from 1.2 to 2.8 inches, in 0.2-inch increments. The travel speed can be set to 0.66, 0.98, or 1.31 feet per second. For track spacing, you can choose between High Efficiency and Precision Cut. For the number of passes, you can choose between one and two. Michael Rupp You can adjust the sensitivity of the N8’s obstacle detection in three levels. The high setting avoids stepping stones and areas covered in leaves. The medium setting avoids stone paths and terrace edges. The low setting avoids only large areas without grass. If you switch off camera detection, you must first set up the pool, raised slabs, and tree roots as restricted zones. The app will remind you of this. The N8 detects rain and pauses for a pre-set period of three hours. It also features schedules, a quiet mode, anti-theft protection, a mower cleaning function, and a dedicated mode for the area around the charging station. Michael Rupp The Sweeping mode is not a third operating mode, but a profile for collection mode with two pre-set passes. Speed and noise levels remain the same. Sweeping doesn’t quite describe the process accurately, as nothing is actually swept up. A tip for autumn: If you just want to clear leaves from the area without cutting the grass, set it to 2.8 inches. As long as the grass remains below this height, the blades barely touch it. Anthbot N8: Collecting and emptying This is where the N8 really shines. The grass catcher fills up without leaving any significant debris behind. Nothing sticks to the soles of your shoes or your dog’s paws anymore. Michael Rupp You don’t have to empty the full collection basket yourself. A sensor monitors the fill level. When the grass box is full, the robot moves to a pre-defined dumping area, tilts the grass box and rear panel upwards, and then carries on working. This also happens at the end of a job or on command via the app. You can set up to five such areas, each at least 5 by 5 feet in size, which can be rotated and resized in the app. One detail: the dumping area must be within the mowing zone. If you’d like it to be somewhere else, simply extend the mowing zone accordingly. Michael Rupp There’s a reason why it’s a discharge area rather than a single point. The N8 discharges in a staggered pattern. This creates several small piles instead of a single cone, which could block the discharge. In our test, the discharge worked without a single failure. Michael Rupp The clippings in the basket are coarser than one might expect. The collection disc cuts once and then conveys the clippings on. It does not shred them. The result is reminiscent of an electric mower with a grass catcher: pieces of grass interspersed with leaves and leaf fragments. The contents of the grass catcher can be composted or put in the organic waste bin. A minor design flaw only becomes apparent when it rains. The upper covering of the collection basket is waterproof and forms a hollow in the center where rainwater collects. This does not hinder mowing or emptying. The water drains out when the basket is tipped. If the robot is in its docking station during a shower, a puddle forms. The original garage only covers the robot itself. The collection basket protrudes from the rear. A drain in the collection basket would be a simple improvement for the next model. Michael Rupp Anthbot N8: Fallen leaves Falling leaves are usually shredded by robotic mowers and often remain visible on the lawn. When there are large quantities, this is more than just a cosmetic issue. The layer of leaves can block out light from the grass, and the organic matter provides food for fungi. Leaves from trees infested with fungi should be removed from the lawn entirely anyway, as mulching spreads the pathogen. This is precisely where the N8 excels thanks to its Cyclone blade disc and collection basket. Michael Rupp On our test lawn, the area that had already been mown was largely clear after a single pass, while the leaves were still lying all over the area right next to it. The area wasn’t completely free of leaves, with a few individual leaves remaining. I can only achieve this level of cleanliness with a hand rake and great effort. The overall result is impressive: I come home from the office in the evening to find the leaves gathered in a small pile at the edge rather than scattered across the lawn. No other robotic lawnmower has managed this on our test course so far. You should clean the grass catcher every now and then with a broom or garden hose to ensure air can escape unhindered. Anthbot N8: Lanes, turning, and edges There’s nothing to complain about when it comes to the mowing result. The N8 cuts parallel lines with a slight striped pattern and covers the area completely. For the evaluation, we set up a 360-degree camera (DJI Osmo 360 II) securely at the edge of the lawn and recorded the process as a time-lapse. This allowed us to track the path, turning maneuvers, and evasive movements over a complete run. Michael Rupp During initial commissioning with an early firmware version, the robot’s behavior at the end of the track seemed erratic. Some tracks were missed, and the mower shut down while turning. Anthbot quickly rectified the issue. With firmware 0.3.90, navigation ran smoothly. Turning maneuvers remain complicated, and this is down to the design. The mower head is rigidly attached to the rear and does not turn with the robot. When the robot turns on the spot, this rear end swings outwards in a wide arc and collides with a wall, fence, or hedge, even though the wheels are free to move. Consequently, the N8 first veers off to the side, reverses, and then turns into the new path. Each end of a track thus requires several maneuvers. This extends the working time and has a greater impact the more turns are required – that is, when the mowing direction is transverse and the track spacing is narrow, and even more so when two passes are made. A strip remains uncut at the edge, up to about 6 inches depending on the distance to walls and obstacles. This is not a weakness of this model. A centrally mounted mower without a swiveling disc or trimmer cannot reach the edge. Three edge passes at the end of each mowing session reduce the width of the strip, but do not eliminate it entirely. Trimmers or hand shears are still required. Michael Rupp Anthbot N8: Obstacle detection On the test course, the N8 avoided a crisp packet, a watering can, fake hedgehogs, and children’s toys. It only recognized the fake dog poo at a cutting height of 1.8 inches and below – in other words, on short grass. The reason for this is the camera position. Taller blades of grass obscure objects that are low to the ground before the detection system kicks in. In this respect, the N8 is roughly on a par with the Navimow i210 LiDAR Pro. The N8 is also fitted with an LED spotlight. We advise against mowing at dusk or at night, as small animals are most active at those times. The schedules in the app offer the necessary settings to avoid this. Anthbot N8: Noise level, speed The N8 delivers on its 4-in-1 promise (mowing, mulching, collection, and leaf clearing) thanks to two distinctive features. The first is its noise level. In collection mode with the grass catcher fitted, we measured just under 68 decibels from a distance of 3.28 feet. This is down to the design. The blade disc and spiral housing work together to generate the airflow, and this requires a certain rotational speed. This cannot be optimized via a software update. When in operation, the N8 sounds like a cordless lawnmower. Michael Rupp The second compromise is the working speed. In one test area, the N8 mowed 1,200 square feet in 97 minutes, which works out at around740 square feet per hour. At the fastest speed setting, the maximum is 1.3 feet per second. You’ve also got to remember that it’s consuming more power in this mode. In another run, mowing an area of 960 square feet used up around 80 percent of the battery charge. With a charging time of 80 minutes, the N8 takes a corresponding number of charging breaks when covering larger areas. Anthbot itself quotes around 2,150 square feet of continuous mowing with the grass catcher fitted. Anthbot N8: Conclusion The Anthbot N8 is a specialist mower, and I mean that as a compliment. As a grass-collecting robotic mower and leaf clearer, it tackles tasks that were previously the preserve of rakes and leaf vacuums. The collection system works thoroughly, the automatic emptying function performed flawlessly in our test, and the app offers plenty of customization options without becoming confusing. The drawbacks stem from its design. The grass catcher makes the robotic mower longer and noisier, and it slows it down. The water trough on the grass catcher cover remains an avoidable blunder. Small, winding gardens with lots of corners are also not suitable for it. Before buying, consider how important grass collection is to you. If you want to leave the clippings on the lawn as fertilizer, you’re better off with the other Anthbot models, depending on the size of your lawn. Anthbot N8: Specifications Model: Anthbot N8 Price: $1,699 Mowing systems: Cyclone disc with three blades for collection | Particle disc with six blades for mulching Cutting width: 7.9 inches Cutting height: 1.2 to 2.8, adjustable in 0.2-inch increments Grass box capacity: 61 gallons, automatic emptying at up to five discharge points Navigation: Full-band RTK with reference station and dual-vision cameras, optional NetRTK via 4G Obstacle detection: AI camera detection, sensitivity in three levels Mowing zones: Up to 30, each with its own cutting height, mowing direction, and detection level Travel speed: 0.7 to 1.3 ft./sec. Battery: 9.2 Ah, 198 Wh, 21.6 V Charging time: 80 minutes Maximum gradient: 24 degrees (45 percent), not tested Noise level: 68 dB in collection mode Dimensions: 24 x 17 x 13.1 without grass catcher Weight: 38.7 pounds Water resistance: IPX6 (robot), IPX5 (charging station) Connectivity: Wi-Fi 2.4 and 5 GHz, Bluetooth, 4G Firmware version: 0.3.90

item.title: Spyware can listen in. This is the Windows setting I always change
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Malware can gain access to more than just documents and apps on your PC. Get infected with a certain kind of virus, and your camera and microphone are fair game, too. You can minimize part of the headache by disabling unused microphones. For example, maybe you have both a dedicated microphone and a webcam with a built-in mic connected—if you disable the webcam’s mic and activate the standalone mic’s mute button, that should block any eavesdropping. Added bonus: You’ll minimize the annoyance of starting Zoom and Teams calls with the wrong mic active. (I swear, for me it’s every. single. time.) How to disable a microphone in Windows PCWorld Head to the Sound settings in Windows ( Settings > System > Sound ). Under Input , click on the audio device you want to disable—this could be a webcam, a headset, or something else. In the individual device’s settings, find General > Audio . Click on the Don’t allow button. Why not just disconnect the cable? Unplugging an audio device from your PC is a valid strategy if you use it rarely. But otherwise, you may run into one of two problems: 1 – You can’t use the device because the audio input is mixed with other signals and routed over a single cable. (Ex: webcam) 2 – Your USB port wears out from frequent use. The second problem is fixable by buying a USB hub that has individual on/off switches . But turning off Windows’ access to a mic is free. Keep antivirus active on your PC! You can disable your microphone(s) as a precaution, but also take steps to avoid getting spyware in the first place. Let your antivirus program scan your system regularly, and avoid shady websites and downloads. Also keep an eye on your browser extensions and apps installed—sometimes, legit ones can turn bad right under your nose.

item.title: Logitech’s new $260 work/leisure headset is also repairable
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Logitech is launching the Zone Vibe Pro , a wireless over-ear headset that’s designed to be used both at work and in your free time. The Zone Vibe Pro doesn’t have a traditional microphone boom, instead using AI-based voice isolation to reduce background noise. The speakers feature 40mm drivers and adaptive active noise cancellation (ANC). With ANC enabled, the battery life is expected to last up to 30 hours with music playback or up to 18 hours with active talk time. Without noise cancellation, the battery life can reach up to 66 hours. A 5-minute charge is all that’s needed to regain about 1 hour of talk time. This headset can be connected to multiple devices via Bluetooth Multipoint, and the sound quality can be customized using the Logi Tune app. Logitech has also made the headband, ear cushions, and battery replaceable to extend the headset’s overall lifespan. Not a bad move given the current state of high-priced consumer electronics. So what exactly makes this headset for work and leisure? Here’s what Logitech says in its announcement post : “Modern professionals working across open offices, at home or on the go, shouldn’t need multiple audio solutions for work and life,” said Joseph Mingori, VP and General Manager of Mobile and Audio Solutions at Logitech. “Zone Vibe Pro solves that problem by giving employees the option of great sound everywhere with comfortable fit while giving IT teams reliable, certified hardware.” The Logitech Zone Vibe Pro is available now for $259.99 in three colors: Black, Graphite, and Off-White. For a limited time, it also comes with a free Logitech Wooden Headset Stand included.

item.title: Microsoft promised a better Windows 11. Here’s its 6-month report card
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
This was supposed to be the year Microsoft fixed Windows 11. Back in March, Microsoft made an unusually blunt promise: Windows would become faster , more reliable, more consistent, and less eager to shove Copilot into every corner of the operating system. Six months later, Windows 11 26H2 is rolling out, and it’s time to grade the results. The early report card? Search earns an A-, Microsoft has done a decent job putting Copilot back in its lane, and Windows feels noticeably quieter. But the Start menu still gets a C, and performance on 8GB PCs remains a work in progress. That makes 26H2 less of a dramatic new beginning than a progress report on Microsoft’s Windows reset. And in several important ways, the company really has listened. Microsoft’s Windows 11 26H2 Update is here, and you should already have it First things first: chances are that you’ve already had a chance to experience Microsoft’s changes for yourself. Though Microsoft now issues a single, major “feature release” each fall, the changes are actually delivered incrementally. Each month, Microsoft delivers some incremental pieces of code as part of its Patch Tuesday updates, which deliver some of these feature improvements on a regular cadence. The fall update rolling out this week simply “rolls up” those changes within a single update, if a user or organization has optionally delayed those changes for whatever reason. And the changes to Windows aren’t necessarily additions, either. In general, they’re a look back to what Windows was , in an era before AI was rampant and the world ran on Windows 10. Let’s get to the grades. Taskbar and Start menu: C In September, Microsoft’s update finally allowed you to move your Windows taskbar to any part of the screen you wish, adjust the size, and tweak items such as badging options for individual icons. Likewise, the Start menu now allows you to resize the individual icons, with separate buttons for Pinned, Recently Used, and All. I hate to say it, but neither change made a profound difference to me. I absolutely give credit to Microsoft for making these changes, if only because it acknowledged that the company was listening to its customers. I briefly noodled with moving the Start menu around within Windows 10; some of the early browser experiments in rearranging tabs made readjusting the Start menu a fun experiment. What Windows 11 ultimately “taught” me was that I didn’t strongly care where my taskbar ended up, and forcing it to the bottom center was something I learned to live with. The Windows 11 Start menu, though, I still truly despise. I really enjoyed how Windows 10’s Start menu combined dynamic live tiles/widgets, which used the large, bright icons to full effect. I would actually use my mouse to navigate either through my array of Live Tiles, or scroll through the alphabetical listing of additional apps. Windows 11’s Start menu used to have that, too! Microsoft pledged to make Start feel faster by moving to WinUI3, and I guess it does. But that’s not really the issue here. Microsoft’s Start menu hasn’t changed much from March, with various categories of apps that Windows arranges. Mark Hachman / Foundry Today, I simply launch new applications by “searching” for them ( Win+[app name] ) and use the app to bring up recent documents. For me, the “Start” menu is now the icons I have pinned to the Taskbar. But if you do happen to use it yourself, it does feel faster now. Teaching Copilot to chill: B I think Microsoft has made progress here. For many, any AI is too much AI, but for a while there, Copilot was everywhere, with its injection into Notepad as its most egregious offense. Now, you don’t see Copilot icons in Notepad, Photos, and the Windows Snipping Tool anymore (thankfully). You still see it within the Copilot application, obviously (where Microsoft has eliminated its goofy avatar ) and within the Microsoft 365 applications, where I think it truly belongs. ( Copilot destroyed its human competition in the Excel World Championship when I recently tested it.) Microsoft has fussed over its application UI, with one change in May and another, more visionary update just a few days ago, with an eye towards using Windows and Microsoft 365 as a home for vibe-coding and autonomous agents. Microsoft The latter effort could lead to trouble, as Microsoft will undoubtedly feel encouraged to show off what those agents can do for you. But for now, Copilot has been corralled into a few specialized applications where it fits naturally. AI also still exists within Paint, where Copilot can be explicitly asked to design stickers or an AI-generated piece of art. And yeah, that still feels a little weird. What I do like are the image-processing tools within Photos, with everything from generative erasing to super resolution. They’re just Copilot without the Copilot brand, and that’s probably the model going forward: just give us useful AI utilities without throwing Copilot in our face — and use the PC’s local resources where possible. It’s AI, but at least AI that you’re asking for. Improved Search: A- Microsoft promised “a more consistent search experience across the Taskbar, Start, File Explorer and Settings,” as well as “clearer and more trustworthy results.” I think it’s delivered. Typing a search term — “Copilot,” say — into the Taskbar’s search box produces clear differences between apps, settings, and documents. Searching within File Explorer, at least on my SSD-equipped PC, can be as quick as lighting, and rarely takes longer than a second or two across my entire laptop. Again, habit has taught me to open the application, and then the file. However, Windows’ search speed now tempts me to do the opposite. It’s seen a big improvement this year. Windows Update and the Out of the Box (OOBE) experience: B Microsoft basically acknowledged that Windows updates were out of control , pledging to move back to a single monthly update. I appreciate that, but the Windows update process now achieves something Microsoft traditionally struggles with: simplicity on the surface, with more complexity hidden underneath. Do I want the latest updates ASAP? A simple toggle enables this. Do I want to delay the update? I can, and select a specific date as well. That’s exactly what many people want. Me too. I appreciate even nerdier options such as selecting optional preview and driver updates, as well as the numerous options to reset your PC when something goes wrong or an update fails. There’s even “quick machine recovery,” an automated process I’ve never been forced to experiment with, thankfully. My only complaint at the moment is that the “delivery optimization” feature that’s existed within Windows for years — designed to share updates locally, without needing to download from an Internet server — has never seemed to work, ever. Windows Update is now simple and manageable. Resetting or setting up a new PC is also supposed to be faster, and it generally is. One of Windows’ new features is its ability to defer updates, delivering you to the desktop faster. I’ve never taken advantage of this, but anything that smooths the process is a step forward. I still don’t entirely like the Windows Insider hierarchy for preview builds, however. While I like the easier way to migrate a PC in and out of Insider builds, the process of selecting “beta” and “experimental” builds, then opting in to a “release preview” update, then picking which of the code bases to use… It’s too convoluted. On the other hand, I don’t really think the corps of Insiders wants yet another change to the program. Windows performance, especially on 8GB PCs: B This is a tough one. I simply couldn’t say for certain whether Windows feels faster without doing a head-to-head comparison with the same hardware. What I will say is that PCWorld has tested a few laptops with 8GB of memory installed, such as the Dell XPS 13 this past August. In my own experience, these affordable PCs — based on Intel’s Wildcat Lake processor and its Project Firefly initiative — feel akin to Chromebooks, capable of performing many basic tasks. Dell’s new $699 XPS laptops are trying to compete with the Apple MacBook Neo. Dell For me, the dividing line between what these PCs can or can’t do falls somewhere between the “required” and “recommended” specifications that software vendors include. Will the application run, and will it run well? I never had any problem with basic Web browsing or the Microsoft Office applications on the 8GB laptops I tried. However, simply opening Microsoft Edge with ten browser tabs sucked up virtually every bit of memory that Windows provided, and even an idle background app affected performance. I think Microsoft has more work to do here, and it may never match Apple in how effectively it aligns its silicon with its operating system and applications. The question is, will it need to? If the memory crunch continues, Microsoft developers will be forced to keep busy. If it evaporates, Windows can begin gobbling up memory once again. A “quieter” Windows: A- I’m sure many readers will disagree with me here, but Windows does feel less intrusive. Microsoft’s pledge to make Windows “quieter” essentially targeted Widgets, the crazy-quilt app that lives in the right-hand corner of your PC. Widgets began as a simple notification of the current forecast, a change in a stock price, or a notable news event, but quickly became a repository for every random bit of information Microsoft’s Bing search engine could dredge up. Windows Widgets don’t feel calm, but they’re more sedate than they were. Fortunately, Microsoft has reined it in once again. I’m sure many readers see no use for Widgets at all (and if I weren’t in media, I’d agree) but Widgets sits quietly to one side. I also haven’t seen many “ads” for Windows features pop up, either. Then again, I kill off pretty much every Windows notification I can , and I think you should, too. That’s my evaluation. What do you think? You can find PCWorld on Facebook , Bluesky , X , and more. Give us your grades.

You don’t have to drop $1,000 to get a laptop that can handle everyday computing, you know. That said, spending $500 wisely matters here. At this price, some laptops make reasonable compromises while others cut way too many corners. For most folks, I’d recommend opting for a laptop with a 1080p display and at least 8GB of RAM (16GB is always better if you can swing it). While you shouldn’t expect premium features at this price point, there are plenty of laptops that offer excellent day-to-day performance. Here are the best ones we’ve found so far. Why you should trust PCWorld for laptop reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name! PCWorld prides itself on laptop experience and expertise. We’ve been covering PCs since 1983, and we now review more than 70 laptops every year. All of our picks have been personally tested and vetted by our experts, who’ve applied not only performance benchmarks but rigorous usability standards. We’re also committed to reviewing PC laptops at every price point to help you find a machine that matches your budget. What to expect from a good laptop under $500 RAM: 8GB is the minimum I’d target; 16GB is a strong buy if you can find it. Display: Aim for a 1080p screen rather than 720p. Processor: Core i3/Ryzen 3 is fine for basic use; Core i5/Ryzen 5 gives you more breathing room. Storage: Prefer an SSD over slower eMMC storage. Battery life: Around 10-12 hours is a good target. Best for: Web browsing, Office, schoolwork, streaming, video calls, and everyday productivity. Not ideal for: AAA gaming, heavy video editing, 3D work, or other demanding workloads. Chromebook or Windows? Choose a Chromebook if most of your work is browser-based; choose Windows if you need desktop apps, broader software compatibility, or more offline flexibility. At this price, you’re not shopping for premium performance, you’re looking for the fewest painful compromises. The all-aluminum build feels as premium as more expensive models, and the A18 Pro chip delivers fast, responsive performance for everyday tasks like writing and streaming. In our review, we noted that apps open quickly and multitasking feels smooth. Battery life is another big win, lasting well over a full workday in real-world use. The 13-inch Liquid Retina display is also sharp at 2408×1506 resolution and bright at 500 nits–a strong combination at this price point. You don’t get the premium extras like Thunderbolt connectivity or a high-end webcam, but that’s not wholly unsurprising for a laptop at this price point. How we test laptops The PCWorld team puts each and every Windows laptop through a series of benchmarks that test GPU and CPU performance, battery life, and overall usability. The idea is to push the laptop to its limits and then compare it against others we’ve tested. Chromebooks, on the other hand, go through a series of web-based tests. For a much deeper look at our review methodology, check out how PCWorld tests laptops . Who curated this article? Hi, I’m Ashley Biancuzzo , and I oversee all laptop and Chromebook coverage at PCWorld. While you’ll see me review Chromebooks on occasion, I’m also really into the broader world of consumer tech. I spend a lot of time writing and thinking about where laptops are headed–from AI and sustainable designs to long-term trends. When I’m not deep in the world of tech, you’ll probably find me gaming, getting lost in a good book, or chilling with my rescue greyhound, Allen. How to choose the best laptop under $500 Ah, here we are at the billion dollar question. Do you spring for a basic Chromebook or go for a Windows laptop with more features? Honestly, it mostly comes down to your lifestyle and what you’re expecting from a laptop under 500 bucks. You’re not gonna get some super-powerful beast at that price, but if you just need something for the basics, there are a lot of decent options out there. Chromebooks, for example, are super budget-friendly and the battery life is awesome. I actually use one myself for work (writing, editing, all that) and it does the job just fine. If you travel a lot, it’s worth going for something that’s nice and light — under three pounds, if possible. Still not sure what to get? No big deal, take your time figuring it out. I’ve put together a list of quick buying tips below. Laptop type: There are many different laptop types that fall in the sub-$500 category: clamshells, 2-in-1s, Chromebooks, and much more. The displays on convertible laptops (aka 2-in-1s), for example, can swing around 360 degrees. This allows you to use the laptop like a tablet. They can also be propped up like a tent for viewing movies or participating in video calls. Chromebooks come in various shapes and sizes, and exclusively run Google’s web-focused Chrome OS. With a Chromebook, all you need is a Gmail account and, boom, you’re in. CPU: When it comes to the sub-$500 Windows laptops, you can expect to find Intel Core i3 or i5 processors. An i5 processor obviously provides a little more oomph. That said, basic office and web work does just fine on a Core i3. For AMD stuff, Ryzen 3 is fine for everyday stuff like web browsing, and Ryzen 5 is a solid all-rounder—kind of like Intel’s i5. On Chromebooks, Snapdragon and Pentium chips usually beat out MediaTek ones. Graphics : Don’t expect great graphics at this price. You’ll mostly get integrated graphics, which is totally fine unless you’re trying to game or do 3D work. RAM: RAM-wise, go for 8GB if you can—it just makes everything smoother. Most Chromebooks come with 4GB, which works, but 8GB is way better if you can swing it. Display size: For screen size, 13 to 14 inches is the sweet spot. Big enough to work on, small enough to carry around. Bigger screens mean more weight (and usually a higher price). Resolution : Don’t settle for less than 1080p resolution. Anything lower just looks kinda blurry, even for basic stuff like Netflix or spreadsheets. Battery life: Battery life? Look for 10 to 12 hours. That’ll get you through most of the day without hunting for an outlet. Ports : It’s nice to have a bunch so you don’t need extra adapters. Look for USB-C and USB-A, and HDMI is cool if you want to hook up to a screen. FAQ 1. What is the best laptop under $500? MacBook Neo (2026) is the best cheap laptop you can get right now, hands-down. Performance is fast and reliable, and battery life is surprisingly good at 13+ hours. It doesn’t cut corners in many areas either, a rarity in a budget machine. 2. What is the best Chromebook under $500? If you want a solid Chromebook under $500, the Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 is fast, smooth with tabs and video calls, has a sharp 1080p screen, and a good HD webcam. It’s just plain simple and reliable. 3. Can I upgrade the RAM or storage on these laptops later? Most laptops under $500 don’t let you upgrade RAM because it’s soldered on, but some do let you swap or add storage. Check before you buy if that stuff matters to you. 4. What’s the difference between a regular laptop and a Chromebook? When people say “laptop,” they usually mean a PC or a Mac. But Chromebooks are laptops too, they just run Google’s Chrome OS instead of Windows or macOS. So, yeah, all Chromebooks are laptops, but not all laptops are Chromebooks. They’re mostly built for Google apps like Drive and Docs, so they work best when you’re online. 5. Are Chromebooks good for gaming? Eh, not really. If gaming’s your thing, you’ll probably wanna look at a Windows laptop or a Chromebook designed for cloud gaming. Both will be more expensive than a basic Chromebook. Most Chromebooks are fine for web games and Android stuff, but that’s about it. With a gaming Chromebook, you will need to subscribe to a cloud gaming service such as GeForce Now and have a reliable internet connection. 6. Can you use integrated graphics for gaming? Yes, some of the latest processors with integrated graphics can run modern PC games at decent enough settings. For example, we found that in our tests, Intel’s latest Iris Xe line of processors with integrated graphics can run some of the latest games at 1080p and 30fps. Unfortunately this is not the case for all integrated graphics and your mileage may vary drastically with older tech. Intel and AMD’s integrated graphics have made huge leaps in recent years with regard to gaming performance. If you’re on a budget or looking for an ultra-thin laptop with integrated graphics you need not worry, you can still game on. How to choose the best gaming monitor Gamers have unique needs that exceed an average user. Here’s what PC gamers should look for in a gaming monitor. Resolution Most widescreen gaming monitors have a resolution of 1920×1080 (1080p), 2560×1440 (1440p), or 4K (3840×2160). A higher resolution improves sharpness and clarity, which helps games look more detailed and lifelike. Increasing resolution also increases demand on your video card, however. Gamers with less powerful hardware may want to avoid 4K. Refresh rate A higher refresh leads to smoother motion by increasing the number of frames that can appear each second. It also reduces input lag, as each frame appears more quickly. A 144Hz refresh rate is a big improvement over the standard 60Hz, and 240Hz is better still. The improvement becomes more difficult to notice after 240Hz, but 360Hz monitors exist for those who want the lowest input lag possible. DisplayPort and HDMI 2. 1 DisplayPort is the best connection for PC gaming. Even DisplayPort 1.4, which is rather old, can support 4K at 144Hz. HDMI 2.1 can handle 4K at 120Hz and is an acceptable connection for PC gaming, though most gamers will use it for a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S game console. FAQ 1. What is the best gaming monitor? The best gaming monitor overall is the MSI MPG 341CQPX . The 34-inch panel joins a field of QD-OLED ultrawides, but stands out from the pack with better HDR, a 240Hz refresh rate, and USB-C port with 98 watts of Power Delivery. 2. What is the best cheap gaming monitor? At less than $200, the Pixio PX248 Wave offers incredible value for gamers. The 1080p/200Hz monitor has all the essentials: good image quality, strong motion clarity, and Adaptive Sync support. 3. What resolution is best for a gaming monitor? Many competitive gamers prefer 1080p resolution because it allows for high frame rates and low input lag even on modest hardware. This also makes it ideal for budget shoppers. 1080p is not as crisp as higher resolutions but, if it allows for higher frame rates, can look good in motion. 1440p remains a great mid-range option. It looks much sharper than 1080p but doesn’t drastically increase load on your video card. A variety of 1440p monitors now support a refresh rate up to 240Hz. 4K is the last word in sharpness and clarity. Playing a modern game on a 4K monitor takes the experience to a new level. It’s very demanding on your video card, however, so you’ll need top-tier hardware for a smooth experience. Ultrawide monitors differ in resolution because they have a wider screen. Most ultrawide monitors have a resolution of 3440×1440, which delivers sharpness similar to a 1440p ultrawide. Some larger monitors have more exotic resolutions: the 49-inch Samsung Odyssey G9 Neo, for example, has 5120×1440 resolution. 4. Should I use AMD FreeSync or Nvidia G-Sync? AMD FreeSync and Nvidia G-Sync can synchronize the refresh rate of a compatible monitor with the output of an AMD or Nvidia video card. This ensures smooth motion and eliminates screen tearing, a distracting visual artifact. You might be surprised to learn that most AMD FreeSync and Nvidia G-Sync monitors rely on the VESA Adaptive Sync standard. This is why many gaming monitors now support both. The difference in performance is minimal. Our G-Sync vs. FreeSync comparison goes in-depth on their similarities and differences. 5. Should I buy an ultrawide gaming monitor? The short answer? Yes . Our top choice, the Alienware AW3423DW, is an ultrawide gaming monitor. An ultrawide aspect ratio is more immersive in racing, simulation, and role-playing games. It also offers a large, more impressive perspective in many strategy games. Not all games support an ultrawide aspect ratio, however. It’s wise to check that your favorite games support ultrawide monitors before making a purchase. Consoles rarely support ultrawide aspect ratios, so console gamers should stick with a widescreen display. item.title: You don’t need max graphics settings for great PC gaming visuals
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
In the world of PC gaming, there’s a persistent myth that, to achieve maximum FPS rates (FPS, frames per second), you generally have to set all graphics settings to their maximum. However, we’ll show you that just a handful of settings are enough to massively enhance the visual experience without placing an excessive strain on modern graphics cards. The absolute standout among these free upgrades is anisotropic filtering. This technique ensures that textures on surfaces at an acute angle to the camera — such as a road leading to the horizon or a tiled floor — remain crystal clear. Without anisotropic filtering, these surfaces appear muddy and blurred at medium and long distances, which severely disrupts immersion. Not all graphics options automatically consume a great deal of processing power. Even simple filters can result in visibly better graphics. Corsair The technical reason for the low power consumption is fascinating: Modern GPUs feature specialized hardware units for texture sampling. As the required texture data is already stored in the extremely fast graphics memory (VRAM), the additional sampling from different angles takes almost no processing time. Whether you set it to ‘8x’ or ‘16x’ often makes a difference of less than one frame per second on current graphics cards, while visual clarity increases dramatically. We therefore strongly recommend that you always force this setting in the driver, as many games use values that are too low by default. For Nvidia graphics cards, right-click on the desktop, open the ‘Nvidia Control Panel’ and navigate to ‘Manage 3D Settings.’ In the native graphics driver (in this case for Nvidia graphics cards), you can generally force the use of anisotropic filtering in applications. Foundry In the ‘Global Settings,’ locate the ‘Anisotropic Filtering’ option and set it to ‘16x.’ Users of AMD graphics cards should open the Adrenalin Edition software, then navigate via the ‘Gaming’ tab to the ‘Graphics’ section and expand the ‘Advanced Options.’ There, please set the anisotropic filtering mode to ‘Override application settings’ and also select the ‘16x’ level. Another important point is the overall texture quality: Many players are wary of the ‘Ultra’ setting, but a simple rule applies here: As long as your graphics card’s video memory is large enough to accommodate the high-resolution texture packs, this setting will not affect performance at all. The graphics card setting ‘Anisotropic Filtering’ ensures that surfaces in games that are at an acute angle to the camera remain sharp. Foundry It is only when the VRAM overflows and data has to be offloaded to the slower system RAM that severe stuttering occurs. The same applies to SSAO, screen-space ambient occlusion. This technique calculates subtle shadows where objects meet. At the same time, it adds depth to the scene so that objects do not appear to be floating in mid-air. SSAO is the resource-efficient variant of ambient occlusion and usually costs modern chips only about 1 to 2 percent of their processing power. If modern post-processing techniques such as TAA (Temporal Anti-Aliasing) make the image appear slightly too soft, you can also use the sharpening filter in the driver. On Nvidia cards, you’ll find it under ‘Image Scaling’ in the global 3D settings. On AMD cards, it’s called ‘Radeon Image Sharpening.’ A setting of around 30 percent is often sufficient to compensate for the blurring caused by TAA and achieve a crystal-clear image without any significant loss of performance.
